_note: The URL a client must build for GET /api/v1/audit/chain/{requestId}, and the
request id the server must recover from it.
This file is the contract between the server and EVERY client, and both sides
assert against it rather than against each other's prose:
server  apps/api/internal/handlers/audit_chain_path_contract_test.go
serves each `path` through a real chi router mounted at `route` and
checks the production decode (handlers.chainRequestID) recovers
`requestId` exactly.
desktop apps/desktop/src/__tests__/lib/audit-chain-api.test.ts
checks api.getAuditChain(requestId) requests exactly `path`.
Why a shared fixture instead of each side hard-coding a string: real
correlation ids CONTAIN A SLASH (chi mints `hostname/b64prefix-000001`), so a
client must percent-encode the id to keep it one path segment. A client that
encodes wrongly does not get an error — it gets an EMPTY chain, which reads as
'this request touched nothing'. A client-side test asserting its own
construction would pass on exactly that bug, because it never asks the server
whether the URL it built round-trips.
The cases are not all realistic ids; some exist to prove the encoders agree
where they could plausibly disagree. JS encodeURIComponent escapes '+' and '='
while Go's url.PathEscape leaves both alone in a path segment — both are valid
and both must decode back to the same id.

cases.name: slash-free id needs no escaping and must still route
the shape chi actually mints: hostname, slash, base62 prefix, counter
characters JS escapes and Go would not — the round trip must still hold
a literal percent and a space survive double-encoding

_note: The same id with its slash left raw. It splits into an extra path segment and
misses the one-segment route entirely, which is why encoding is mandatory
rather than cosmetic.
